title: Scheduling Fundamentals
summary: Why a CPU scheduler exists and the exact metrics used to judge any scheduling algorithm, with a worked Gantt-chart example.

slides.markdown:
A **CPU scheduler** decides which ready process runs next whenever the CPU is free — after a process blocks, finishes, or its time slice expires. Every scheduling algorithm you'll study (FCFS, SJF, Round Robin, MLFQ) is really just a different answer to the same question: given several processes wanting the CPU, who goes next and for how long?

This topic gives you the metrics — turnaround, waiting, response time — you'll use to judge every algorithm that follows, and the vocabulary (preemptive, dispatcher) that frames how scheduling actually happens.

slides.sectionTitle: Why the CPU needs a scheduler
slides.markdown:
With more runnable processes than CPU cores — true on almost every real machine, almost all the time — something has to decide the order and duration each process gets to run. Without a scheduler, you'd need one process to finish entirely before another starts, which is unacceptable the moment any process does I/O and would otherwise leave the CPU idle waiting.

The scheduler's job is exactly this arbitration: keep the CPU busy with useful work, and choose an order that serves whatever goal matters — fairness, throughput, responsiveness, or meeting deadlines, depending on the system.

This is the resource-manager job from [What Is an Operating System](what-is-an-operating-system) applied specifically to the CPU — the scarcest, most contended resource in most systems.

**Non-preemptive** scheduling only lets the running process give up the CPU voluntarily — by finishing, or by blocking on I/O. Once a decision is made, the scheduler can't take the CPU back until that process is done or blocks itself. **Preemptive** scheduling lets the OS forcibly interrupt a running process — most commonly via a hardware timer interrupt — and hand the CPU to someone else, even mid-execution.

Nearly every general-purpose OS today is preemptive: it's the only way to guarantee that one runaway or CPU-hogging process can't starve everything else indefinitely, since the scheduler doesn't have to wait for that process's cooperation.

The trade-off is overhead: every preemption is a context switch, which costs real cycles — so preemptive scheduling buys fairness and responsiveness at the price of switching overhead that non-preemptive scheduling avoids entirely.

The **scheduler** decides *which* process runs next; the **dispatcher** is the code that actually does the switch — saving the old process's registers and program counter, loading the new process's saved state, switching memory mappings, and jumping to the new process's next instruction.

The time this takes is **dispatch latency**, and it's pure overhead: no useful application work happens during it. On typical hardware this runs in the low microseconds, but it's paid on every single context switch, so a scheduler that switches too aggressively can spend a meaningful fraction of total CPU time just dispatching rather than running anything's actual code.

This is exactly why quantum size (how long a process runs before Round Robin preempts it, covered later) is a real engineering trade-off, not an arbitrary knob — too small a quantum means dispatch latency starts to dominate.

slides.sectionTitle: Scheduling criteria: utilization, throughput, turnaround, waiting, response time
slides.markdown:
Five metrics let you judge any scheduling algorithm precisely instead of vaguely. **CPU utilization** — the percentage of time the CPU is doing useful work, not idle. **Throughput** — completed processes per unit time. **Turnaround time** — total time from a process's arrival to its completion (`completion − arrival`). **Waiting time** — total time a process spends in the ready queue, not running (`turnaround − burst time`). **Response time** — time from arrival to the *first* time it gets the CPU, distinct from turnaround.

Different algorithms optimize different subsets of these, often at each other's expense — which is exactly why "which scheduler is best" has no universal answer, only "best for which metric."

The worked example on the next slide computes several of these directly so the formulas stop being abstract.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: Gantt-chart timeline showing these metrics
slides.markdown:
![FCFS Gantt chart with waiting and turnaround times](assets/fcfs-gantt-chart.svg)

For this schedule: P1 waits 0 (starts immediately at its arrival), P2 waits 4 (arrives at 1, starts at 5), P3 waits 6 (arrives at 2, starts at 8). Turnaround times: P1 = 5, P2 = 7, P3 = 8. Average waiting time = (0+4+6)/3 ≈ 3.33.

Every scheduling algorithm in this group produces a Gantt chart exactly like this one — the algorithm just changes the order and lengths of the blocks.

slides.sectionTitle: Turnaround time vs response time — optimizing for different users
slides.markdown:
These two metrics can pull an algorithm in opposite directions, which is why systems have to pick a priority.

| | Turnaround time | Response time |
|---|---|---|
| Measures | Arrival to completion (the whole job) | Arrival to first CPU burst (how fast it "starts") |
| Matters most for | Batch jobs — nightly reports, video encoding | Interactive jobs — typing in an editor, clicking a button |
| Good algorithm example | SJF/SRTF — finishes short jobs fast overall | Round Robin — everyone gets the CPU quickly, if briefly |
| Bad example for this metric | Round Robin can worsen average turnaround by chopping long jobs into many slices | FCFS can leave short interactive jobs waiting behind one long job |

**How to decide which to optimize for:** ask whether a human is watching and waiting on the *first* sign of progress (response time) or only cares when the whole job is *done* (turnaround) — a compiler build cares about turnaround, a terminal keystroke cares about response time.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: optimizing average turnaround while starving individual jobs
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Minimizing average waiting time is always the right goal — just pick whichever algorithm's average is lowest."

**Why it's wrong:** an average hides its distribution. An algorithm that gives 99 processes near-zero wait and one process an enormous wait can have a fantastic average while being genuinely broken for that one process — this is exactly what happens to long jobs under Shortest Job First once a steady stream of short jobs keeps arriving (see the next topic's starvation discussion).

**Correct model:** report and care about *worst-case* wait alongside the average, not just the average. Production schedulers explicitly guard against this with mechanisms like **aging** (raising a waiting process's priority over time), because "great on average, terrible for one unlucky job" is not an acceptable trade-off for a general-purpose system.

slides.sectionTitle: Senior nuance: fairness metrics beyond the classic five
slides.markdown:
Modern schedulers (Linux CFS, covered in depth in Scheduling in Practice) explicitly optimize for a sixth property the classic five don't capture well: **fairness over a time window** — did every process get its proportional share of CPU time recently, not just "on average since it started."

CFS tracks each task's **vruntime** (virtual runtime, roughly "CPU time consumed, weighted by priority") and always picks the task with the least vruntime to run next — which mathematically tends toward equal vruntime across tasks over time, a much stronger and more precise notion of fairness than "low average waiting time."

The distinction matters in an interview: naming turnaround/waiting/response time shows textbook knowledge; naming that production schedulers optimize a fairness metric over a *sliding window*, not lifetime averages, signals you've looked past the textbook.

slides.sectionTitle: How this shows up in production
slides.markdown:
`vmstat` and `top` surface scheduling metrics directly: the load average reflects how many processes are runnable but waiting for the CPU (a proxy for queueing delay), and a process's `%CPU` combined with high perceived latency despite low CPU usage often points to it spending time in the ready queue, not actually blocked — exactly the waiting-time metric from this topic, visible on a live system.

API gateways and thread pools face the identical trade-off as CPU schedulers at a different layer: a pool that processes requests strictly FCFS can leave a fast, cheap request waiting behind a slow, expensive one — the same convoy effect a CPU scheduler fights, just one layer up in an application's own request-handling code.

Recognizing scheduling metrics outside the kernel — in thread pools, job queues, request routers — is a transferable skill this topic is really teaching, not just OS trivia.
